Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette: Amir had always taken pride in his work as a firefighter, but that sense of security was shattered when he became the target of a stalker. It started with small things - finding strange notes on his locker at the fire station, receiving hang-up calls on his phone - but escalated to the point where Amir would catch glimpses of this person lurking around his neighborhood or following him on his daily bike commute. As time passed, certain physical locations began to trigger a cascade of memories and emotions. The streets he used to ride his bike with ease now filled him with dread, making him feel like he was being watched and followed. Even the fire station, once a safe haven, became a source of anxiety as he would scan the area for any sign of this person. Amir's mind began to replay the memories of these encounters without warning, transporting him back to that state of hyper-vigilance. He'd feel overwhelmed by emotion, unable to find words to describe what had happened. The experience left an indelible mark on Amir, leading him to believe he had permanently changed for the worse. "I'm not the same person anymore," he would say to himself. This notion fueled a deep-seated fear that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy. He couldn't shake off the feeling of weakness that had settled in - if only he had been stronger, more capable, this wouldn't have happened. As Amir navigated his daily life, these negative appraisals only intensified his sense of threat. Loud noises made him jump, and he found himself constantly scanning exits whenever he entered a room or building. His eyes would dart towards other people, searching for any signs that they might be a danger to him. Even the sound of sirens, once a call to action, now sent a chill down his spine. Amir's wife began to notice the change in him, but he struggled to articulate what was happening inside his mind. He couldn't find words to describe the memories that haunted him - all he knew was that they were suffocating him. His reactions, once a natural response to a traumatic event, now felt like evidence of his own weakness. As the months went by, Amir's behavior became more erratic, causing tension in his relationship with his wife and affecting his performance at work. He began avoiding social gatherings and stopped riding his bike altogether, fearing that he would be putting himself in harm's way again. But these attempts to regain control only seemed to reinforce the cycle of fear and anxiety. Amir's thoughts became consumed by a constant, gnawing sense of threat - if he wasn't vigilant enough, this person could still find him. His memories continued to resurface without warning, each time bringing with them a fresh wave of emotion that left him reeling. The more he struggled to make sense of it all, the more convinced he became that his reactions were a sign of impending madness. It was only when Amir's wife sat him down and expressed her concern for his well-being that he realized he couldn't keep going on like this. He knew he needed help, not just to manage his symptoms but to challenge the negative appraisals that had taken hold of him. With a heavy heart, Amir made the decision to seek professional help, hoping that somehow, someway, he could break free from this cycle and reclaim his life.
